item.title: Weather pushes back SpaceX's Crew-12 window, opening door for first ULA launch of year
item.description: NASA's plans to get the first human spaceflight of the year off the pad have to hold off until at least Friday because of weather constraints along the flight path needed in case of emergency. That delay, though, opens the door for a national security mission aiming for liftoff on Thursday morning.

item.title: Nature is a powerful ally against fires and floods: So how can it be saved?
item.description: More than a year after the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, the economic aftershocks of the disaster still permeate the lives of the people who survived it. Fewer than a dozen homes in some of the city's hardest-hit neighborhoods have been fully rebuilt. Families remain scattered across temporary rentals, and many are still grappling with letters from their insurers announcing higher premiums, reduced coverage or no renewal at all.

item.title: OpenAI policy exec who opposed chatbot’s “adult mode” reportedly fired on discrimination claim
item.description: The executive has denied the allegation that she engaged in discrimination.

item.title: NASA selects two Earth System Explorers missions
item.description: Two next-generation satellite missions announced Thursday will help NASA better understand Earth and improve capabilities to foresee environmental events and mitigate disasters.

item.title: Study reveals floods are the biggest drivers of plastic pollution in rivers
item.description: Plastic pollution has become a major global environmental concern as modern societies rely increasingly on plastic products. Much of this plastic waste eventually reaches the ocean, with rivers acting as the main transport routes from urban, agricultural, and other landscapes, thereby affecting the lives of marine organisms.

item.description: Even as the US steps back from Paris and New Zealand flirts with imported gas, the global energy transition is gathering speed.

item.description: A new report claims the e-commerce giant is looking to create a pipeline of licensable content between media publishers and AI companies.

item.title: An ice dance duo skated to AI music at the Olympics
item.description: Czech ice dancers Katerina Mrazkova and Daniel Mrazek are learning the hard way that LLMs sometimes spit out straight-up plagiarism.

item.title: Where did that raindrop come from? Climate model ensemble captures worldwide water isotopes over 45 years
item.description: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, and sometimes these atoms are slightly heavier than usual. These heavier forms are called isotopes. As water evaporates or moves through the atmosphere, the amount of these isotopes changes in predictable ways. This can act as a fingerprint, allowing researchers to trace the movement of water at global scales.

item.description: Robert Playter announcd he is leaving Boston Dynamics after 30 years at the company in various roles, including six years as CEO.

item.title: Old galaxies in a young universe?
item.description: The standard cosmological model (present-day version of "Big Bang," called Lambda-CDM) gives an age of the universe close to 13.8 billion years and much younger when we explore the universe at high-redshift. The redshift of galaxies is produced by the expansion of the universe, which causes emitted wavelengths to lengthen and move toward the red end of the electromagnetic spectrum.

item.title: Top medical groups join forces to review vaccine science as CDC faces criticism
item.description: The American Medical Association is launching an effort to evaluate vaccine safety and effectiveness independently of U.S. government health agencies

item.description: Out of the twelve-person founding team, only seven are still at the company (counting Elon).

item.title: Underestimated wake: Shipping traffic causes more turmoil in the Baltic Sea than expected
item.description: Commercial shipping not only affects the Baltic Sea on the surface, but also has a significant impact on the water column and the seabed. A study by the Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW) and Kiel University (CAU) now shows for the first time that wake turbulence from large ships in heavily trafficked areas of the western Baltic Sea significantly alters water stratification and leads to marked sea floor erosion. The research team has therefore documented a previously underestimated human impact on shallow marine areas. The results are published in the journal Nature Communications.

item.title: Facebook adds new AI features, animated profile photos, and backgrounds for text posts
item.description: Facebook's new AI features let users animate their profile pics, restyle their Stories and Memories, and add backgrounds to text posts.

item.description: DDoS hit blog that tried to uncover Archive.today founder's identity in 2023.

item.title: Trace gases play previously unseen role in cloud droplet formation, research reveals
item.description: Tiny, invisible gases long thought to be irrelevant in cloud formation may actually play a major role in determining whether clouds form—and possibly whether it rains.

item.description: Tony Wu leaves a company now entangled with social media, space-based IPOs.

item.title: Europe's Ariane 6 to launch Amazon constellation satellites into orbit
item.description: An enhanced version of Europe's Ariane 6 rocket will blast off Thursday to launch 32 satellites into orbit, forming part of the Amazon Leo network, which it hopes will rival Elon Musk's Starlink.

item.title: Windows' original Secure Boot certificates expire in June—here's what you need to do
item.description: PCs without the new certificates could eventually have trouble booting new OSes.

item.title: Which humans first made tools or art – and how do we know?
item.description: Building the human story based on a few artefacts is tricky – particularly for wooden tools that don’t preserve well, or cave art that we don’t have the technology to date. Columnist Michael Marshall explores how we determine what came first in the timeline of our species

item.title: Hubble captures light show around rapidly dying star
item.description: This stunning image from NASA's Hubble Space Telescope reveals a dramatic interplay of light and shadow in the Egg Nebula, sculpted by freshly ejected stardust. Located approximately 1,000 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus, the Egg Nebula features a central star obscured by a dense cloud of dust—like a "yolk" nestled within a dark, opaque "egg white." Only Hubble's sharpness can unveil the intricate details that hint at the processes shaping this enigmatic structure.

item.title: When blackouts occur during heat waves, Austin homes pose major risk
item.description: If the power goes out during a heat wave, there's nowhere more dangerous to be than where people spend most of their time—indoors. A new study led by researchers at The University of Texas at Austin is the first to assess the indoor heat vulnerability for each single-family home in an entire city. The research used Austin as its testbed, but the approach can be applied to most cities in the U.S.

item.description: Once considered an oddity of quantum physics, time crystals could be a good building block for accurate clocks and sensors, according to new calculations

item.description: The Results About You tool is getting an upgrade.

item.title: Earth’s core may contain 45 oceans’ worth of hydrogen
item.description: An experiment to quantify the amount of the universe’s lightest element in Earth’s core suggests that the planet’s water has mostly been here since the beginning

item.title: Scientists may have discovered a pulsar at the Milky Way’s heart—a result that could reveal new physics
item.description: If a pulsar that may lie at the center of our galaxy is confirmed, it could enable more precise measurements of the spacetime around the Milky Way’s central supermassive black hole

item.title: The Kia PV5 electric van combines futuristic looks and thoughtful design
item.description: Forget VW's expensive retro bus—this is the electric van we've been waiting for.

item.title: How teaching molecules to think is revealing what a 'mind' really is
item.description: Networks of molecules in our body behave as though they have goals and desires. Understanding this phenomenon could solve the origins of life and mind in one fell swoop

item.title: Chang'e-6 samples constrain lunar impact flux and illuminate early impact history
item.description: Scientists from the Institute of Geology and Geophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), the CAS Aerospace Information Research Institute, and other institutions, have revised the decades-old lunar crater chronology model, using samples collected from the far side of the moon by China's Chang'e-6 mission and complementary remote sensing imagery.

item.title: Vega raises $120M Series B to rethink how enterprises detect cyber threats
item.description: Vega Security raised $120 million Series B, bringing its valuation to $700 million, in a round led by Accel. The company aims to rethink how enterprises detect cybersecurity threats.

item.title: Launch to ISS delayed again over weather: NASA
item.description: NASA is now aiming to launch four astronauts to the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday, in another delay over weather conditions, the U.S. agency announced Tuesday.

item.title: US to scrap cornerstone of climate regulation this week
item.description: President Donald Trump's administration is expected to finalize this week its repeal of a foundational scientific determination that underpins the US government's authority to regulate greenhouse gas pollution.

item.title: Discovery of a possible pulsar in the Milky Way's center could enable unprecedented tests of General Relativity
item.description: Researchers from Columbia University and Breakthrough Listen, a scientific research program aimed at finding evidence of civilizations beyond Earth, have published new results from the Breakthrough Listen Galactic Center Survey, one of the most sensitive radio searches ever conducted for pulsars in the dynamically complex central region of the Milky Way. The study, led by recent Columbia Ph.D. graduate Karen I. Perez, was published in The Astrophysical Journal.

item.title: A possible first-ever Einstein probe observation of a black hole tearing apart a white dwarf
item.description: On July 2, 2025, the China-led Einstein Probe (EP) space telescope detected an exceptionally bright X-ray source whose brightness varied rapidly during a routine sky survey. Its unusual signal immediately set it apart from ordinary cosmic sources, triggering rapid follow-up observations by telescopes worldwide.

item.title: Moving beyond money to measure the true value of Earth science information
item.description: They're all around us: sensors and satellites, radars and drones. These tools form vast remote sensing networks that collect data on the climate, the ground, the air, and the water. This information is immensely useful for research, conservation, and disaster preparedness. But, according to an interdisciplinary group of Earth science researchers in a paper led by Casey O'Hara of UC Santa Barbara, we're only just scratching the surface of understanding just how beneficial Earth science information can be.

item.title: Old EV batteries could meet most of China's energy storage needs
item.description: Electric vehicle batteries are typically retired once they reach about 80 per cent of their original capacity, but they could be repurposed in electricity grids to balance out slumps in renewable generation

item.title: Hauler Hero collects $16M for its AI waste management software
item.description: Hauler Hero has seen its customer base, revenue, and head count double since the company raised its seed round in 2024.

item.title: India orders social media platforms to take down deepfakes faster
item.description: India’s new rules take effect February 20, tightening deepfake oversight and shrinking takedown windows to as little as two hours.

item.title: How your worldview can affect the Earth through three values
item.description: The ways people interact with and view nature speak volumes as to how Earth is treated, and the severity of environmental concerns rising makes what shapes people's view of nature a pertinent topic. Understanding how and why people might be motivated to protect nature is no small feat. Researchers have been able to present a study on 745 Japanese participants using three types of nature's value—intrinsic, relational, and instrumental—to categorize a method to fully appreciate what goes into the construction of a human's relationship with nature.

item.title: Alphabet selling very rare 100-year bonds to help fund AI investment
item.description: Alphabet becomes first tech company to issue 100-year bonds in nearly three decades.

item.title: Plants and worms harnessed to improve sustainable urban drainage systems
item.description: A team of researchers has demonstrated how biological systems could transform the way sustainable urban drainage systems manage polluted soils, pointing to a future in which urban infrastructure is greener, cheaper and more resilient. The project, led by the University of Strathclyde with partners Phyona Ltd and Pictish Worms, is using plants and worms to regenerate contaminated soils.

item.title: Former GitHub CEO raises record $60M dev tool seed round at $300M valuation
item.description: Thomas Dohmke's new startup offers an AI system to allow developers to better manage all the code AI agents produce.

item.title: AI video startup Runway raises $315M at $5.3B valuation, eyes more capable world models
item.description: Startup Runway has raised a $315 million round at a $5.3 billion valuation, funds it will use to expand beyond AI video generation and into world models.

item.title: Non-biologic processes don't fully explain Mars organics collected by Curiosity, researchers say
item.description: In a new study, researchers say that nonbiological sources they considered could not fully account for the abundance of organic compounds in a sample collected on Mars by NASA's Curiosity rover. The paper is published in the journal Astrobiology.

item.title: How giant galaxies could form just 1.4 billion years after the Big Bang
item.description: The existence of massive, elliptical galaxies in the early universe has puzzled astronomers for two decades. An international team led by Nikolaus Sulzenauer and Axel Weiß from the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy (MPIfR) used data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to shed light on this open question of galaxy formation. They studied one of the most spectacular galaxy aggregations in great detail and published their results in the current issue of The Astrophysical Journal.

item.title: Experiment relies on pulsars to probe dark matter waves
item.description: Dark matter is a type of matter that is predicted to make up most of the matter in the universe, yet it is very difficult to detect using conventional experimental techniques, as it does not emit, absorb, or reflect light. While some past studies gathered indirect hints of its existence, dark matter has never been directly observed; thus, its composition remains a mystery.

item.title: January 2026 fifth warmest on record despite cold snap in Europe, North America
Fermi data help refine orbital parameters of a gamma-ray binary
item.description: Using NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, Chinese astronomers have observed a gamma-ray binary system known as PSR J2032+4127. Results of the new observations, published February 3 on the arXiv preprint server, shed more light on the orbital parameters of this binary, which could help us better understand its nature.

item.title: China's emissions policies are helping climate change but also creating a new problem
item.description: China's sweeping efforts to clean up its air have delivered one of the biggest public health success stories of recent decades. Since the Air Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan was launched in 2013, coal-fired power plants have been fitted with scrubbers, heavy industry has been modernized and pollution standards tightened, leading to an over 50% reduction in atmospheric particulate matter.

item.title: Why 1.5°C failed and setting a new limit would make things worse
item.description: Setting a limit for global warming didn't succeed in galvanising climate action quickly enough – now we should focus on making the annual average temperature rise clear for all to see, says Bill McGuire

item.title: What came before the big bang?
item.description: Physicists cannot access anything that existed before the start of time and space, but they have theories

item.title: The quirky geology behind Olympic curling stones
item.description: The rocks used in the Olympic sport of curling come from one island in Scotland and one quarry in Wales. What makes them so special?

item.title: January was fifth hottest on record despite cold snap: EU monitor
item.description: The planet experienced its fifth-hottest January on record despite a cold snap that swept across the United States and Europe, the EU's climate monitor said Tuesday.

item.title: Warming climate threatens Greenland's ancestral way of life
item.description: Standing in his boat with binoculars in hand, hunter Malik Kleist scans the horizon for seals. But this February, the sea ice in southwestern Greenland has yet to freeze, threatening traditional livelihoods like his.

item.title: Half of the world's coral reefs suffered major bleaching during the 2014–2017 global heat wave, estimates suggest
item.description: Benefits to society from coral reefs, including fisheries, tourism, coastal protection, pharmaceutical discovery and more, are estimated at about $9.8 trillion per year. For the first time, an international team led by Smithsonian researchers estimated the extent of coral bleaching worldwide during a global marine heat wave, finding that half of the world's reefs experienced significant damage. Another heat wave began in 2023 and is ongoing.

item.title: Rules of mysterious ancient Roman board game decoded by AI
item.description: A Roman stone board game has been unplayable since its discovery more than a century ago, but AI might have just worked out the rules

item.title: An emotional countdown to the maiden launch of the Ariane 64, Europe's most powerful rocket
item.description: In a tightly controlled manufacturing hangar west of Paris, workers put the finishing touches on an enormous silver-colored engine. In just a few days, a similar machine will help propel the most powerful version of Europe's Ariane 6 rocket yet, flying for the first time with four boosters.

item.title: The first signs of burnout are coming from the people who embrace AI the most
item.description: Because employees could do more, work began bleeding into lunch breaks and late evenings. The employees' to-do lists expanded to fill every hour that AI freed up, and then kept going.
